ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Prosthodontics Consultation — George Washington — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week review, seen the same day by prosthodontics: the oral ulcers, the diagnosis and the plan for new dentures and a two-implant lower overdenture

text.paragraph: Complete edentulism with complete dentures more than eight years old that are loose and painful and make eating and public speaking difficult, in a 57-year-old head of government with 6% weight loss over six months and two ulcers under the lower denture. Please assess the jaws, ulcers and dentures and advise on new dentures and implant options. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks, on the day of his two-week primary care review. [S]

list.item: Are the ulcers denture trauma, and does anything in the mouth need a biopsy?
Can the present dentures be adjusted, or should they be replaced?
Is he a candidate for an implant-retained lower overdenture, and what assessment and sequence do you advise?
What interim measures will help him eat and speak in public until treatment is complete?
What maintenance and recall will he need?

text.paragraph: Mr. Washington, a 57-year-old head of government, is seen at the request of Dr. Pritchard-Boateng. He lost his teeth gradually over about thirty years and has worn complete dentures for more than eight years. The lower denture has become loose and painful; it lifts when he chews or speaks, and the upper clicks. He has limited his diet to soft food and lost weight. For two weeks he has kept the lower denture out except at meals, and the soreness has gone. He cleans the dentures daily. He has never used tobacco and has no diabetes or bone-modifying treatment. His work requires frequent public speaking and dining. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: George Washington was born on February 22, 1732, at Popes Creek farm in Westmoreland County, Virginia (February 11 in the Julian, or Old Style, calendar then in use in England and its colonies). [D]

In November 1751, at 19, on his only journey outside mainland North America, he went to Barbados with his older half-brother, who was seeking relief from tuberculosis; there he wrote that he was "strongly attacked with the small Pox," was in bed for about three weeks, and recovered with slight scarring and lifelong immunity. [D]
Through his adult life he had repeated attacks of malarial fever, a common summer and autumn illness at Mount Vernon, which he treated with Peruvian (cinchona) bark. [D]

In June 1755, as an aide on the Braddock expedition, he had dysentery with "violt Fevers & P[ai]ns in my h[ea]d," travelled lying in a wagon, rode into battle on cushions, and took about five weeks to recover; the National Library of Medicine exhibition says he nearly died of it. [D]

He had poor dental health from his twenties, with regular toothaches, decay and tooth loss; at 24 he paid a "Doctr Watson" to remove a tooth, and through his life he wrote of aching teeth, lost teeth, inflamed gums and ill-fitting dentures and bought toothbrushes, scrapers, toothache medicine and cleaning solutions. [D]

By 1781, missing several teeth, he wore false teeth wired to his remaining natural teeth; a dentist treated him in New York in 1783, and he sent a wax and plaster model of his mouth to a dentist so that more false teeth could be made. [D]

In May 1784 his plantation accounts recorded a cash payment to enslaved people at Mount Vernon for nine teeth, "on acc[oun]t of the French Dentis Doctr Lemay," a dentist then visiting the area and offering tooth transplants. Mount Vernon reads the entry as teeth bought for the dentist, does not know whether any were later used for him, and notes that the threat of punishment was always present for enslaved people, so that they could have felt compelled to provide them. [D]

When he was inaugurated as president in 1789, only one natural tooth remained. That year a New York dentist made the first of four sets of full dentures for him, of hippopotamus ivory with human teeth, gold wire springs and brass screws, leaving a hole for the remaining tooth. [D]
All his dentures caused him pain and changed the shape of his face, pushing out his lower lip, and he found them difficult to use when eating or speaking. [D]

The four surviving dentures include hippopotamus, walrus and probably elephant ivory; cow, horse and human teeth; and lead, brass, silver, gold and small wood pegs. Two contain human teeth, whose source is unknown: Mount Vernon writes that dentists then kept a stock of teeth bought from poor people, enslaved or free, or taken from the dead, and that teeth from enslaved people may be in them but no record shows it. [R]
To try to avoid an early death he exercised, ate and drank moderately, tried to get enough sleep, and avoided tobacco. [D]

He was inaugurated as the first president at Federal Hall in New York on April 30, 1789, and lived at 3 Cherry Street until February 1790, when the household, which included his family, many enslaved workers and often some of his advisers, moved to a larger house at 39 Broadway. [D]

Less than two months after the inauguration he had "a very large and painful tumor on the protuberance of my thigh" that kept him from walking or sitting; after weeks of treatment, two physicians, father and son, removed it on June 17, 1789, and the wound took six weeks to heal, while he lay mostly on his right side. A similar, milder tumor returned two years later. [D]

What the 1789 thigh tumor was is not settled in the sources read. Mount Vernon calls it a tumor; the National Library of Medicine exhibition lists anthrax among his serious illnesses without saying when; the roster calls it a carbuncle. [R]
In New York in January 1790 his diary records that he was "At home all day—not well" on January 17 and on January 18 "Still indisposed with an Aching tooth, and swelled and inflamed Gum." [D]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Denture-related traumatic ulcers (K12.1). The ulcers healed within two weeks once the denture was out between meals, which confirms trauma from the overextended, unstable lower flange. No lesion needs a biopsy; any ulcer that persists for two weeks after the cause is removed would. [S]

Complete edentulism, ACP diagnostic index class III (K08.103). Complete edentulism of both jaws, class III by the American College of Prosthodontists diagnostic index because of the mandibular bone height of about 14 mm and the unfavorable lower ridge and muscle attachment. The worn dentures with a closed bite account for the pain, the instability and the change in the support of his lips. Relining the old dentures would not correct the worn teeth or the bite, so replacement is advised. [S]

Implant candidacy (K08.103). The McGill and York consensus statements make a two-implant overdenture the first-choice standard for the edentulous lower jaw, with better chewing, comfort and satisfaction than a conventional denture. He is healthy, does not smoke, has no diabetes and takes no bone-modifying drug, and the panoramic radiograph suggests enough bone in the canine regions; a cone beam CT will confirm it. The upper denture is expected to do well without implants on his well-formed upper ridge. [S]

Nutrition and speech (R63.4). Poor chewing explains his narrowed diet and weight loss. New dentures need a few weeks of adaptation for chewing and speech; the lower denture will stay less stable than the upper until the attachments are connected. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Pritchard-Boateng's intake note: weight 92.4 kg, down about 5.6 kg in six months; MNA-SF 10; hemoglobin A1c 5.4%, albumin 3.7 g/dL, blood count, metabolic panel, TSH and vitamin B12 normal. Panoramic radiograph today: edentulous jaws without retained roots or bony lesion; mandibular bone height about 14 mm at the symphysis, with the mental foramina close to the crest. Weight today 92.8 kg. [S]

list.item: Relieve the lower flange and reline the old lower denture with a tissue conditioner today, and keep it out overnight. [S]
New upper and lower complete dentures over the next four weeks, the lower designed for conversion to an implant overdenture, with an adjustment visit 24 hours to one week after delivery. [S]

Cone beam CT of the mandible, then two implants in the lower canine regions after the new dentures are delivered, with amoxicillin 2 g one hour before surgery, chlorhexidine rinses for two weeks and a short course of ibuprofen; the denture relieved and soft-lined over the implants; sutures out at about ten days. [S]
Connect stud attachments to the implants after about three months of healing, with a check within a week. [S]
Read aloud daily with the new dentures; a speech-language assessment if speech is not clear by six weeks. [S]
Continue the soft high-protein diet with the supplement until chewing is restored, and widen the diet as the new dentures settle. [S]

Clean the dentures daily with a soft brush and non-abrasive cleanser, keep them out overnight in water, and attend a yearly prosthodontic recall; replace the attachment inserts when retention falls. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Pritchard-Boateng, who saw him the same day. The diagnosis, the options of conventional dentures alone or with two lower implants, and the time needed for each step were explained to Mr. Washington, who asked how long he would be without dentures and chose the implant plan after learning he would never be without them. [S]

Follow-up: Prosthodontics will make and deliver the dentures, place the implants and connect the attachments, then see him yearly; Dr. Pritchard-Boateng continues his medical and nutritional care. [S]
